entry.evidence: How tectonic plates slip slowly and episodically along their boundaries, is a major, open question in earthquake science.

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

steps.action: The authors pose the open question of how slow slip works and note that the proposed role of pore pressure has never been observed, because deep fault processes are hard to link to near-surface pore-pressure measurements.
steps.quote: it has never been observed because of the difficulty in linking deep processes at seismogenic depths with near-surface pore-pressure measurements

steps.action: The authors take from the subduction-zone literature the hypothesis that slow slip events are causally linked to changes in fluid activity at the fault zone.
steps.quote: have led to the hypothesis of a causal relationship between SSEs and changes in fluid activities at the fault zone

steps.action: The authors take from prior work the regional setting: deep creep in the western MMF from repeating earthquakes, 9–16 mm/yr aseismic creep at the Western High from acoustic ranging, and seeps and a mud volcano within the fault damage zone.
steps.quote: aseismic creep rates of 9–16 mm/year16 were measured in the Western High area

steps.action: The authors use free-fall differential piezometers from their own earlier work (refs 22, 49), with sensor accuracies of ±0.5 kPa and 0.05 °C.
steps.quote: two differential piezometers22 measuring pore pressures in excess of hydrostatic pressures

steps.action: Two piezometers were deployed from October 2013 to November 2014, one within the MMF valley (PZS) and one close to the mud volcano (PZN), to monitor the coupling between hydrogeology and tectonics.
steps.quote: to investigate the coupling between the hydrogeological and tectonic systems along the WH segment of the MMF

steps.action: Two earthquakes struck during the monitoring period and supplied the conditions: the Mw 4.8 2013EQ on the MMF 12.5 km from PZN and the Mw 6.9 2014EQ 209 km away.
steps.quote: During the monitoring period, two notable earthquakes occurred

steps.action: The authors decomposed seven years of public NGL GPS time series from five stations with STL and found that TEKR north and up displacements are perturbed after the 2013EQ, while the other stations follow the regional trend.
steps.quote: we used the STL (seasonal-trend decomposition based on LOESS)29 procedure in R30

steps.action: Excess pore pressure at PZN-P6 rises for more than 3.5 months starting about one week after the 2013EQ, then becomes negative; PZS-P5 turns negative one week after the 2013EQ for 2.5 months; only these sensors show sustained changes.
steps.quote: Excess pore-pressure data (i.e., above hydrostatic) measured at 7.08 mbsf (PZN-P6) and 6.28 mbsf (PZS-P5) show two opposite trends

steps.action: The authors back-analysed penetration dissipation curves with cavity expansion theory to obtain hydraulic diffusivity, then solved a 1D diffusion–advection equation by finite differences for three fluid velocities to infer the hydraulic regime above PZN-P6.
steps.quote: Three values of vz are considered showing that pure diffusion (vz = 0 m/s) is needed to reproduce the general trend of PZN-P5 data

steps.action: The authors compared PZN-P6 and PZN-P5 pore pressures with the effective lithostatic stress from the core density profile and inferred hydro-fracturing at PZN-P6 during the first five months.
steps.quote: PZN-P6 pore-pressure peaks are reaching 70–100% of σ’v before dropping sharply

steps.action: The authors used Tekirdag daily mean temperature as a reference for the TEKR vertical signal, confirming its seasonal origin and isolating a 10-month locked period after the 2013EQ.
steps.quote: confirms the seasonal origin of the geodetic vertical component

steps.action: The authors compared PZN-P6 pore pressure with the seasonally corrected TEKR north displacement and found that they synchronize after the 2013EQ, with a 0.35 cm northward shift from the pre-event trend.
steps.quote: pore pressure recorded by PZN-P6 synchronizes remarkably well with the TEKR GPS northern displacement

steps.action: The authors rejected, by argument, a local shallow process as the common cause of the two signals and concluded that shearing along the fault disturbs both.
steps.quote: a shallow localized process at the level of the piezometer is impossible to be detected by onshore GPS data and vice versa

steps.action: The authors propose that the mud volcano acts as a window that links stress and strain changes in the seismogenic zone to shallow pore pressure.
steps.quote: We propose that this is due to the MV, which acts as a window to the MMF seismogenic zone

steps.action: The authors hypothesize that the PZS-P5 negative pore pressure records shear dilatancy caused by aseismic creep along the MMF, as the shallow expression of deeper creep.
steps.quote: may be the result of an aseismic creeping activity along the MMF, which occurred in response to dilatancy due to shearing

steps.action: The authors checked the dilatancy premise against lithology: P5 sits in a silty–sandy layer identified from core density and P-wave logs, and the five PZS sensors in clay show no perturbation.
steps.quote: the other five sensors at PZS positioned within clayey sediments did not show any pore-pressure perturbation during the monitoring period

steps.action: Using an Okada elastic half-space dislocation model of the discretized MMF (158 × 7 cells), the authors computed TEKR displacements for four source cases (pure versus mixed right-lateral/tensile slip, east-to-west versus west-to-east propagation) at a range of depths.
steps.quote: To test the shear-dilatancy hypothesis, we use a numerical model to describe the SSE.

steps.action: The authors compared the simulated general trends of north and vertical displacement at TEKR with the observed sequence (north then south; up then subsidence).
steps.quote: the only simulations that match these trends is the case where the rupture propagates from east to west and rupture occurs at a shallow depth

steps.action: The authors excluded west-to-east propagation (cases B and D) and deeper slip surfaces (below 6 km for pure strike slip, below 8 km for mixed slip) as inconsistent with the TEKR trends.
steps.quote: Supplementary Table 1 summarizes all the simulations and whether they conform to the aforementioned trends

steps.action: From the best fit (case C), the authors estimated a shallow slipping patch (<8 km) with a transient inflation component propagating east to west at 0.5 km/day, and slip of 0.6 cm (mixed) or 0.2 cm (pure strike slip), equivalent to M5.3 or M5.1.
steps.quote: the value that provided the best fit to the observations was a velocity of 0.5 km/day

steps.action: The authors compared the best-fitting shallow slip scenario with published results from the same region.
steps.quote: These best fitting scenarios of a shallow slipping event are consistent with results from the literature obtained from the same region16,38,39

steps.action: Faced with a predicted positive east–west displacement absent from the TEKR data, the authors attributed the mismatch to model auxiliaries (uniform slip, homogeneous elastic medium, or amplification by normal faults) rather than to the slip hypothesis.
steps.quote: [...] , predicts an east–west positive displacement not detectable on the TEKR data

steps.action: The authors mapped the PZS-P5 pore-pressure record onto the longitude of the propagating slip front and found that the 50-day dilatancy coincides with slip along the Western High segment (S1).
steps.quote: it is found that the 50-day recorded dilatancy occurred during a slipping event along the WH segment of the MMF

steps.action: The authors set the field result beside laboratory measurements of pore-pressure transients in isolated faults (Proctor et al.) and dilatancy theory (Segall & Rice).
steps.quote: Our field data confirm the role of such pore fluid‐sediment interactions in controlling or accompanying the process of fault slipping.

steps.action: The authors keep a timeline scenario in which shallow aseismic slip propagates east to west for more than 10 months, causing shear dilatancy, reactivating the mud volcano, and producing the TEKR displacements.
steps.quote: This aseismic slipping event propagates along the MMF at 0.5 km/day from east to west lasting more than 10 months.

steps.action: The authors leave open whether the slow slip event started with the 2013EQ or triggered it.
steps.quote: it is not possible to ascertain when or where this 10-month SSE has nucleated

steps.action: The authors relate the result to published work on Western High seismic clustering, numerical fault dilation, San Andreas SSEs, and pore-pressure waves and fault valving, and claim direct support for the latter.
steps.quote: provide direct evidence supporting this proposition

tree.answer: Yes: TEKR geodetic disturbance and opposite pore-pressure transients after the 2013EQ
No: slip at depth is not observed; it is inferred from one GPS station and two piezometers
Explain the pore-pressure/deformation coupling by creep-induced shear dilatancy
Partly: a local shallow process is rejected by argument; kinematic rivals are source type, propagation direction and depth (cases A–D)
Yes for direction and depth (different TEKR trends); pure strike slip at 0–6 km also matches, so dilatancy is not singled out by geodesy
Found: a live 2013 earthquake and slow slip during the monitoring period

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No: one event, one GPS station, two piezometers
Partly: seasonal and lithology controls and depth sensitivity; east–west mismatch handled by protecting auxiliaries; slip size not robust to cell size
Kept as best explanation: shallow east-to-west slow slip with creep dilatancy

end.claim: After the 2013 Mw 4.8 earthquake, a more than 10-month shallow aseismic slip event propagated east to west along the Main Marmara Fault at about 0.5 km/day; creep-induced shear dilatancy coupled near-fault sediment pore pressure (including mud volcano reactivation) with far-field displacement at TEKR.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the comparison showing that PZN-P6 pore pressure synchronizes with the seasonally corrected TEKR north displacement after the 2013EQ, there would be no coupling to explain and no slow slip event to model.

gates.evidence: Action: the piezometers were deployed 'to investigate the coupling between the hydrogeological and tectonic systems' (§2 ¶1), which is an aim rather than a stated hypothesis; the GPS data are public archive data analysed afterwards; the shear-dilatancy hypothesis is stated only after the data are described (§2.2 ¶1). Claim: the dislocation model could have failed to match the TEKR trends, and west-to-east and deep cases did fail (§4.7 ¶4). However, the pure strike-slip case also matches at 0–6 km, so the dilatant component is not tested by geodesy, and the east–west misfit was absorbed by auxiliaries (§2.3 ¶1). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data; the propagation velocity is the best-fit value (§4.7 ¶6).

imports.item: STL seasonal-trend decomposition based on LOESS (Cleveland et al. 1990), run in R
cavity expansion theory and pile/cone penetrometer pore-pressure dissipation analysis (Burns & Mayne 1999) to derive hydraulic diffusivity
centered explicit finite-difference scheme for the 1D diffusion–advection equation
Tekirdag daily mean temperatures from climexp.knmi.nl as a seasonal reference

novelty_claims.quote: it has never been observed because of the difficulty in linking deep processes at seismogenic depths with near-surface pore-pressure measurements
Our data provide clear confirmation that regional strain (TEKR GPS data) and near-surface sediment pore pressure (PZN-P6) are interconnected
provide direct evidence supporting this proposition

limits: (1) The claim rests on one GPS station (TEKR) and two piezometers during one event. No statistical measure of the synchronization between pore pressure and displacement is given; the match is visual (Figure 4, p. 5). (2) Geodesy does not single out the dilatant component: pure right-lateral slip at 0–6 km also matches the TEKR trends (§4.7 ¶4). Dilatancy rests on the pore-pressure data and lithology (inference). (3) The model's predicted east–west displacement is not observed. It is explained by untested auxiliaries (variable slip, normal faults) that 'would require more complex models and data for validation' (§2.3 ¶1). (4) Sub-claims at other statuses: the 0.5 km/day propagation velocity and the shallow (<8 km) depth are estimate_with_resolution, but no uncertainty is reported. Slip size is explicitly not concluded (§4.7 ¶5). Hydro-fracturing at PZN-P6 and the mud volcano 'window' are best_explanation. The nucleation question (SSE before or after the 2013EQ) is no_conclusion (§3 ¶2). The pressure drop 4 days before the 2013EQ is only suggestive (§3 ¶4). (5) §3 ¶1 attributes the shear-dilatancy record to 'PZN-P5' where §2.2–§2.3 use PZS-P5. This is probably a typo (inference). §2.3 ¶1 writes 'TERK' for TEKR. (6) The supplementary information (Supplementary Table 1, Supplementary Figs. 1–16) and the peer review file were not supplied, so Methods-only checks are coded from the text alone and no review sequence is coded. The paper states that reviewer reports are available. (7) The order of decisions is not documented: whether the hypothesis preceded the GPS analysis cannot be told from the text (inference). (8) Composition is none_fits. Conditions are found in a live event, not traces, so trace_series does not strictly apply. There is no repetition across events, so natures_repetition does not apply. The rival cases differ only in kinematics and do not all fail a shared crucial test, so strong_inference does not apply. The walk is observation, then a post hoc hypothesis, then model fitting, then a best explanation. (9) Future deployments of piezometers along transform faults are proposed (§3 ¶4) but not performed.

disagreements.target: Several authors who suggested a fluid–tectonic stress relationship from indirect evidence (refs 5, 17, 20, 36)
disagreements.support: The paper offers concurrent in situ pore-pressure and GPS records as direct evidence for a link previously inferred indirectly.
disagreements.quote: Several authors have suggested, based on indirect evidence, a relationship between fluid activities and tectonic stresses5, [...] .

disagreements.target: Rousset et al. 2019: slow slip events on the San Andreas fault detected only at depth (>16 km), lasting 3–20 [...]
disagreements.support: The paper reports a 10-month SSE on a transform fault at shallow depth (<8 km), from dislocation modelling of TEKR data.
disagreements.quote: Shorter duration (3–20 days) SSEs have been detected along the San Andreas fault, however only at depth (>16 km)46.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Case C: right-lateral slip with a transient tensile (inflation) component, propagating east to west, shallow (<8 km)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Case A (pure right-lateral, east to west), Case B (pure right-lateral, west to east), Case D (mixed, west to east), each at a range of depths
alternatives_considered.reason: Only east-to-west shallow cases match the observed TEKR north and vertical trends; the dilatant case is retained on the basis of piezometer observations

alternatives_considered.chosen: None chosen; the hypothesis is kept and the model simplification is blamed
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Spatially variable slip (less slip on the eastern section) versus amplification of north–south motion by normal faults north of the MMF
alternatives_considered.reason: These scenarios would require more complex models and data for validation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Cells of 2 km × 2 km on a vertical fault, a single active cell, no normal faults
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Larger or smaller cells, multiple cells at different depths with different slips, inclusion of normal faults near the MMF
alternatives_considered.reason: none given; the authors state these may change the slip values and so draw no conclusion on slipping-zone size

alternatives_considered.chosen: Inflation contributions not summed across cells (transient, active only during slipping)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Summing inflation contributions from all elements (permanent inflation)
alternatives_considered.reason: Based on observations at PZN and PZS that inflation is a transient phenomenon

alternatives_considered.chosen: Alternation between pure diffusion and diffusion–advection above PZN-P6
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Three vertical fluid velocities, including pure diffusion (vz = 0) and vz = 3 × 10−8 m/s
alternatives_considered.reason: Pure diffusion reproduces the general trend at PZN-P5, while advection is needed for the observed peaks

alternatives_considered.alternatives: The SSE started with the 2013EQ, or the 2013EQ was triggered by the SSE
alternatives_considered.reason: Not possible to ascertain from the available data
